newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says it did not know of bomb suspect's record.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says it did not know of bomb suspect's record.

text.p: The Immigration and Naturalisation Service said on Sunday it did not know that one of the men charged with plotting to bomb New York subways was a suspected Islamic extremist when he was released from custody in February.

"We had no information whatsoever this man was a terrorist," INS spokesman Brian Jordan said. He also said that an immigration judge, who was not part of the INS, made many of the decisions in the case of Gazi Ibrahim Abu Mezer, including granting an asylum hearing and lowering his bail.

New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani complained on Saturday that the INS should not have allowed Abu Mezer, 23, to be released after he asked for asylum on grounds that Israel would persecute him as a suspected member of a "known terrorist organisation."
"I think it is appropriate to question why this person was allowed into the country announcing that he was part of a terrorist group in Israel," the mayor said.

Mezer and Lafi Khalil, 22, were arrested in a Thursday morning raid of a Brooklyn apartment where five bombs were found. Police said they shot the two suspects in the raid as they reached for weapons.

According to Jordan, the INS let Abu Mezer return voluntarily to Canada the first two times they caught him trying to illegally enter the country through the state of Washington. But the third time, in January 1997, they detained him.
According to a U.S. Justice Department official, Canada refused to allow him to return because Abu Mezer had been convicted of using stolen credit cards and assault in Canada.
Jordan said the INS then tried to deport Abu Mezer to a third country, but "for reasons we still can't understand" the immigration judge lowered his bail from $15,000 to $5,000.
Another Middle Eastern man, who is in jail on unrelated charges, paid the bail, immigration sources told Reuters.

In April, Jordan said, Abu Mezer asked for political asylum. The judge agreed to a hearing in January 1998, but in June Abu Mezer withdrew the request for asylum and was given a standard 60 days to leave the country, Jordan said.
Whether the men were acting on their own or were supported by another group remains an important issue in the investigation.
Law enforcement sources said the suspects were using phones in their local laundromat and grocery store to call the Palestinian resistance movement Hamas. Hamas denied any link.
